Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- Cambodia and Thailand have agreed to redeploy some troops away from the site of a border temple at the center of a tense military standoff in its second week. Thai soldiers take a rest near the Preah Vihear temple in Preah Vihear province. The decision came after the two sides met to resolve the impasse. Government officials from both nations plan to meet again to decide how many troops will remain at the site of the Preah Vihear temple, the Thai News Agency reported Monday. At a later meeting, the two sides plan to discuss how to tackle the thorny issue at the center of the ongoing dispute -- the question of whether land around the temple belongs to Thailand or Cambodia. The 11th century temple sits atop a cliff on Cambodian soil but has its most accessible entrance on the Thai side. The two countries differ on whether some territory around the temple forms part of Thailand or Cambodia. The decision to redeploy troops took place after a Monday meeting in Siem Reap, Cambodia. Last week, an eight-hour meeting between Thai and Cambodian officials ended with both sides agreeing on only one point: that troops each country has amassed at the site of the temple will not fire on each other. The International Court of Justice awarded the temple to Cambodia in 1962. Thailand claims, however, that the 1.8 square mile (4.6 sq. km) area around it was never fully demarcated. Thailand says the dispute arose from the fact that the Cambodian government used a map drawn during the French occupation of Cambodia -- a map that places the temple and surrounding area in Cambodian territory. This month, the United Nations approved Cambodia's application to have the temple listed as a World Heritage Site -- a place the U.N. says has outstanding universal value. The decision re-ignited tensions, with some in Thailand fearing it will make it difficult for their country to lay claim to disputed land around the temple. Opposition parties in Thailand used the issue to attack the government, which initially backed the heritage listing. Cambodian Prime Minister Hun Sen, who has been in power since 1985, portrayed the U.N. recognition as a national triumph in the run-up to the general elections. Analysts believe that the nationalist sentiments stirred up by the military standoff helped Hun Sen's ruling party win enough seats in Sunday's parliamentary elections so that it can form a government without the need for a coalition. The current flare-up began July 15, when Cambodian guards briefly detained three Thais who crossed into the area. Once they were let go, the three refused to leave the territory. Cambodia claims Thailand sent troops to retrieve the trio and gradually built up their numbers. Thailand denies that, saying its troops are deployed in Thai territory.

# Cambodia and Thailand Move to Ease Tensions Over Preah Vihear Temple Dispute

Cambodia and Thailand have reached an agreement to redeploy a portion of their military forces away from the contested area surrounding the Preah Vihear temple, marking a tentative step toward de-escalation as the standoff between the two nations enters its second week. The agreement comes after days of heightened military presence along the border, which had raised concerns about the potential for the situation to spiral into open conflict.

As part of this de-escalation process, government officials from both countries are scheduled to convene again in the near future. Their immediate priority will be to negotiate and finalize the specific number of troops that will remain stationed at the site, even as forces are drawn back. This meeting is being viewed as a preliminary step, one that must be resolved before the two sides can turn their attention to the more complex and longstanding territorial dispute that lies at the heart of the crisis.

## The Root of the Dispute

At the center of this conflict is a fundamental disagreement over sovereignty: specifically, whether the land immediately surrounding the ancient Preah Vihear temple belongs to Thailand or to Cambodia. This question persists despite a landmark 1962 ruling by the International Court of Justice, which awarded ownership of the 11th-century temple itself to Cambodia. While that ruling settled the matter of the temple's ownership, it left unresolved the status of the surrounding territory, a gap that has fueled decades of intermittent tension between the two neighbors.

Thailand's position rests on the assertion that the 1.8-square-mile area encircling the temple was never definitively demarcated. Thai officials have specifically challenged the validity of a map dating back to the French colonial era, which Cambodia relies upon as the primary evidence supporting its claim to the disputed land. This disagreement over historical boundaries and colonial-era documentation has proven to be a persistent obstacle to resolving the territorial question, even as both nations have generally respected the ICJ's original decision regarding the temple structure itself.

## Renewed Tensions in Recent Weeks

The current standoff was triggered this month when the United Nations approved Cambodia's application to designate Preah Vihear as a World Heritage Site. While intended as a recognition of the temple's cultural and historical significance, this decision had unintended diplomatic consequences. Thai officials expressed concern that granting this international status to the temple could inadvertently strengthen Cambodia's broader territorial claims, potentially undermining Thailand's position in any future negotiations over the surrounding land. This apprehension quickly translated into heightened military posturing along the border, setting the stage for the tense standoff that has now persisted for more than a week.

As both nations prepare for further diplomatic engagement, the immediate troop redeployment represents a modest but significant gesture toward reducing the risk of escalation, even as the underlying territorial dispute remains far from resolved.

# Cambodia and Thailand Agree to Partial Troop Withdrawal Amid Preah Vihear Border Dispute

Military and diplomatic representatives from Cambodia and Thailand convened in Siem Reap this week for high-level talks aimed at defusing a tense standoff that has seen thousands of troops from both nations stationed along their shared border near the ancient Preah Vihear temple complex.

The 11th-century Khmer temple, perched dramatically on a cliff in the Dangrek Mountains, has long been a source of friction between the two Southeast Asian neighbors. Although an international court ruling decades ago awarded the temple itself to Cambodia, the surrounding land has remained a point of contention, with both countries claiming overlapping territorial rights.

Tensions escalated sharply after UNESCO granted Preah Vihear World Heritage status, a designation Cambodia had long sought as a matter of national pride and cultural recognition. Thai officials, however, viewed the listing with alarm, arguing that it could be used to bolster Cambodian claims over the disputed border areas surrounding the temple, effectively undermining Thailand's own territorial position. In the weeks following the UN announcement, both governments moved additional troops to the border, raising fears of a potential armed confrontation in a region already sensitive to nationalist sentiment on both sides.

Against this backdrop, the talks held in Siem Reap represented a significant diplomatic effort to pull back from the brink. According to officials involved in the negotiations, both sides agreed to begin redeploying a portion of their forces away from the most contested positions near the temple, a move seen as a good-faith gesture intended to lower the immediate risk of conflict.

Importantly, the agreement reached does not resolve the underlying dispute. Rather, it establishes a framework for continued dialogue, with both governments committing to further rounds of talks to address the specific number of troops that should remain in the area and to work toward a longer-term resolution of the territorial disagreement itself.

Analysts and regional observers have cautiously welcomed the development, characterizing it as a meaningful, if incremental, step toward de-escalation. The dispute has drawn concern from other members of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), which has historically emphasized regional stability and non-interference, but has faced pressure to encourage a peaceful resolution given the potential for the standoff to destabilize an otherwise economically vital border region.

For now, the partial withdrawal and commitment to further negotiations offer a fragile but welcome pause in hostilities. Both Phnom Penh and Bangkok have signaled a willingness to continue engaging diplomatically, even as the deeper questions of sovereignty and historical claims over the land surrounding Preah Vihear remain unresolved, leaving open the possibility that tensions could resurface should future talks falter.

# Tensions Simmer at Preah Vihear as Cambodia, Thailand Reposition Forces

**Border Region, Cambodia-Thailand** — Military tensions along the contested frontier near the Preah Vihear temple have flared again, with both Cambodia and Thailand confirming fresh troop movements in the area this week, raising concerns among regional observers about the potential for renewed clashes at one of Southeast Asia's most persistent flashpoints.

## Troop Movements Reported

Defense officials from both countries have acknowledged reinforcing positions near the 11th-century Hindu temple complex, though each side has characterized the moves as defensive in nature. Cambodian military spokespersons stated that additional units were deployed to "protect sovereign territory" following what they described as incursions by Thai forces into disputed zones surrounding the temple. Thai officials, in turn, said their repositioning was a "proportional response" to Cambodian activity near the border and emphasized that Thailand remains committed to a peaceful resolution.

Local residents on both sides of the border have reported increased military traffic, temporary road closures, and heightened security checkpoints. Some villages near the frontier have seen partial evacuations as a precautionary measure, though no large-scale displacement has been confirmed by either government.

Regional diplomatic sources say both nations have maintained communication through military hotlines to prevent miscalculation, but the underlying dispute — rooted in colonial-era mapping discrepancies — remains unresolved.

## A Century-Old Dispute

The standoff traces its origins to the early 20th century, when French colonial authorities, then administering Cambodia, drew border maps that placed Preah Vihear temple within Cambodian territory. Thailand has periodically contested the accuracy of those maps, arguing that the watershed line — a natural geographic boundary — should determine sovereignty, which would place the temple on the Thai side.

In 1962, the International Court of Justice (ICJ) ruled in favor of Cambodia, awarding it sovereignty over the temple itself, though the surrounding land remained ambiguously defined. That ambiguity has fueled decades of intermittent friction.

Tensions escalated sharply in 2008 after Preah Vihear was designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site, a move Cambodia celebrated but which Thailand viewed as a unilateral assertion of control over disputed land. Sporadic gunfire exchanges between 2008 and 2011 killed dozens of soldiers and civilians and displaced thousands of villagers on both sides. In 2011, Cambodia returned to the ICJ, which issued a clarifying ruling in 2013 affirming Cambodian sovereignty over the temple and instructing Thailand to withdraw forces from the immediate vicinity.

Despite that ruling, the precise demarcation of the surrounding 4.6-square-kilometer area has never been fully settled, leaving the region a recurring source of nationalist tension exploited periodically by domestic political actors in both countries.

## Regional and Diplomatic Reactions

The Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), of which both Cambodia and Thailand are members, has historically been reluctant to intervene directly in bilateral border disputes, citing its principle of non-interference. Analysts say this latest escalation could test that posture, particularly if skirmishes result in casualties.

"This is a dispute that never fully goes away — it simmers, and periodically it boils over, often correlating with domestic political pressures in Phnom Penh or Bangkok," said one regional security analyst, speaking on background. "Both governments have incentives to appear strong on sovereignty, which complicates de-escalation."

The United Nations and several foreign ministries, including those of the United States and China, have called for restraint. Beijing, which maintains close ties with both Phnom Penh and Bangkok, is seen as having particular interest in preventing instability along a corridor increasingly relevant to regional infrastructure and trade projects.

## What Comes Next

Cambodian and Thai military commanders are reportedly scheduled to hold border committee talks in the coming days, though no date has been officially confirmed. Analysts caution that while both governments have strong incentives to avoid a repeat of the deadly 2008–2011 clashes, nationalist sentiment and unresolved territorial ambiguity mean the situation could deteriorate quickly without sustained diplomatic engagement.

For now, residents near Preah Vihear are left watching a familiar cycle unfold — one where an ancient temple, revered by both nations, continues to sit at the center of a very modern geopolitical standoff.

*This is a developing story. CNN will continue to update as details emerge.*

# Tensions Flare Along Cambodia-Thailand Border as Historic Grievances Resurface

**Bangkok/Phnom Penh** — Long-simmering tensions between Cambodia and Thailand have escalated in recent weeks, reviving a territorial dispute rooted in colonial-era border demarcations and reigniting nationalist sentiment on both sides of the frontier.

## A Dispute Decades in the Making

At the heart of the conflict lies the ancient Preah Vihear temple, an 11th-century Hindu-Buddhist complex perched dramatically atop a cliff in the Dangrek Mountains. The site has been a flashpoint for generations, despite a landmark 1962 ruling by the **International Court of Justice (ICJ)** that awarded sovereignty over the temple itself to Cambodia.

That ruling, however, left the surrounding land — roughly 4.6 square kilometers — in a legal gray zone that neither Bangkok nor Phnom Penh has ever fully accepted as settled. Thailand has periodically contested the precise demarcation of the border in the area, arguing that colonial-era French maps used in the ICJ's decision were imprecise.

## UNESCO Listing Reignites Old Wounds
